title: The Untold Story of Matthew
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Matthew
Nobody invites tax collectors to dinner unless they want something from them.
That was the world Matthew lived in.
He sat beside coins stained with betrayal. Roman silver. Jewish tears. The sound of sandals scraping across dusty roads while mothers pulled their children closer whenever he looked up.
People did not merely dislike men like Matthew. They considered them contaminated. Traitors. Thieves. Collaborators with pagan oppression. A man who sold his soul one coin at a time.
And maybe that is what makes this story dangerous.
Because deep down, many people secretly believe Jesus only chooses clean people. Disciplined people. Good people. People who already look holy.
But Matthew destroys that illusion forever.
His story begins in the dirt.
And maybe yours does too.
The Gospel writers mention him briefly, almost quietly. But hidden inside those few verses is one of the most emotionally devastating transformations in all Scripture.
In Matthew 9:9, the text says:
“Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And he rose and followed him.”
Simple. Short. Almost too short.
But the original Greek carries a force many modern readers miss.
The phrase “Follow me” is:
ἀκολούθει μοι (akolouthei moi)

This was not casual advice. It was a commanding invitation into total surrender. A call to abandon an old identity. A call to walk behind someone permanently. Not admire Him from a distance. Not agree intellectually. Follow.
And Matthew did. Immediately.
No negotiation. No delay. No cleanup process.
That matters. Because religion often says: “Change first… then maybe God will accept you.”
Jesus said: “Come first.”
That changes everything.
Most people never stop to ask what Matthew actually left behind.
He was likely wealthy. Tax collectors under Rome often became rich through overcharging citizens. The Jewish people viewed them as legalized extortionists.
The Greek word used for tax collector is:
τελώνης (telōnēs)
This was not a respected accountant. This referred to someone associated with greed, corruption, ritual uncleanness, and betrayal against their own people.
Matthew was not merely unpopular. He was socially exiled.
Which means when Jesus called him… everyone watching probably felt uncomfortable.
Because Jesus walked directly toward the man everyone else avoided.
The holy man moved toward the hated man.
And this is where the Gospel becomes personal.
There are people reading this who know exactly what it feels like to carry labels that follow you everywhere.
Divorced. Addicted. Liar. Cheater. Failure. Hypocrite. Unclean. Too far gone.
You learned how to smile publicly while privately believing God probably tolerates you at best.
Matthew understood that feeling.
Yet Jesus looked directly at him. Not through him. Not around him. Not past him.
At him.
The Hebrew understanding behind the idea of being “seen” carries enormous weight throughout Scripture. One connected expression appears in Genesis when Hagar calls God:
אֵל רֳאִי (El Roi)
“The God who sees me.”
Notices me. Knows me. Understands me.
Matthew was seen.
And being truly seen by Jesus is terrifying before it becomes healing.
Because Christ sees what religion hides. He sees the greed. The secret lust. The fake spirituality. The bitterness. The performance. The exhausted pretending.
Yet He still says: “Follow me.”
That is grace.
Not approval of sin. Not indifference toward evil. Grace.
The kind of grace that confronts your darkness while refusing to abandon you inside it.
Many believers imagine the disciples as naturally righteous men. But look closer.
Peter had instability. Thomas had doubt. James and John had pride. Simon had revolutionary extremism. Matthew had corruption.
The kingdom of God was built with broken people.
That should give someone hope tonight.
Especially the person secretly wondering whether God could still use them after everything they have done.
The answer is hidden in Matthew’s own name.
The Hebrew form connected to Matthew is:
מַתִּתְיָהוּ (Mattityahu)
Meaning: “Gift of Yahweh.”
Imagine the irony.
Society saw a traitor. God saw a gift.
People saw his worst chapter. Jesus saw his calling.
And some of you are still defining yourselves by chapters Jesus already paid for.
Matthew’s conversion was not merely emotional. It became visible. Immediate. Practical. Public.
Luke’s Gospel reveals that after following Jesus, Matthew hosted a large banquet. And who attended?
Tax collectors. Sinners. Outcasts. People rejected by religious elites.
Because transformed people immediately begin bringing broken people toward Jesus.
This is one reason authentic Christianity spreads. Not through performance. Not through image management. But through rescued people telling other drowning people where mercy can be found.
The Pharisees hated this scene.
In Luke 5:30 they complained:
“Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
Notice their assumption.
Religious pride always fears contamination. Jesus carried compassion instead.
Christ responded:
“It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
The Greek word for repentance is:
μετάνοια (metanoia)
This does not merely mean feeling guilty. It means a transformative change of mind, heart, direction, and allegiance.
Real repentance is not self-hatred. It is surrender.
And Matthew surrendered everything.

History suggests Matthew eventually carried the Gospel far beyond Israel. Ancient church traditions connect his ministry to regions like Ethiopia or Persia. Though some details remain debated historically, the early church overwhelmingly remembered Matthew not as a corrupt tax collector… but as a faithful witness to Christ.
That is redemption.
Jesus did not merely improve Matthew. He rewrote him.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is this:
Matthew became the writer of the Gospel that bears his name.
The man once known for recording financial transactions became the man recording the words of the Messiah.
The hand that counted stolen coins eventually wrote:
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
Can you imagine the tears behind that sentence?
Matthew understood spiritual poverty. He knew what it meant to feel bankrupt inside.
Which is why his Gospel constantly emphasizes mercy, fulfillment, forgiveness, and the Kingdom of Heaven.
No wonder. He had personally tasted rescue.
And this is where many modern Christians misunderstand discipleship.
Jesus did not save Matthew because Matthew became impressive. Jesus saved Matthew while he was sitting at the tax booth.
Before the sermons. Before ministry. Before spiritual maturity. Before the Gospel account.
Christ loved him first.
The Apostle Paul later echoes this truth in Romans 5:8:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Still sinners. Not cleaned-up versions. Not edited versions. Real sinners.
That means no addiction shocks God. No hidden habit surprises Him. No failure disqualifies someone willing to repent.
But repentance matters.
Modern culture wants a Jesus who affirms without transforming. Scripture never presents that version.
The same Christ who welcomed Matthew also changed Matthew.
Biblical grace does not excuse darkness. It rescues people out of it.
And maybe this article found you at the exact moment you needed that reminder.
Because some people reading this have spent years pretending.
Pretending your heart is okay. Pretending your faith is alive. Pretending your secret sin is under control. Pretending you are not exhausted.
Matthew’s story exposes the truth: Jesus already sees everything.
And He still calls.
Still invites. Still forgives. Still restores.
But there is another layer many overlook.
Tax booths were places of permanence. People sat there daily. It became identity. Routine. Lifestyle. Security.
Matthew walked away from financial certainty into total dependence on Christ.
That is discipleship.
The Greek concept behind discipleship involves more than belief. The word μαθητής (mathētēs) means learner, follower, apprentice.
Christianity was never meant to be passive admiration of Jesus. It was always intended to become transformation through following Him.
And following Christ costs something.
For Matthew, it cost reputation, career, wealth, and old alliances.
For modern believers, it may cost approval. Relationships. Comfort. Addictions. Compromise. Double lives.
But what Jesus gives is infinitely greater.
Because the tax booth could make Matthew wealthy. But only Christ could make him free.
Somebody needed to hear that.
Money cannot heal shame. Attention cannot remove guilt. Pleasure cannot resurrect the soul. Only Jesus can.
And perhaps this is why Matthew’s story still grips hearts thousands of years later.
Because beneath the historical details is a terrifyingly personal question:
What is your tax booth?
What are you still sitting at while Jesus is calling?
Pride? Pornography? Bitterness? Control? Unforgiveness? Secret compromise? Spiritual apathy?
Everyone has something they cling to.
Matthew stood up.
Will you?
They need to know Matthew’s story did not end at the tax booth.
Because one encounter with Jesus can rewrite an identity the world thought was permanent.
